newsitem.title: USA: NYS Gov again slams Democrats for "spending spree".
newsitem.headline: NYS Gov again slams Democrats for "spending spree".

text.p: New York State Gov George Pataki, seeking to quiet criticism that the state's budget likely would be late again, on Tuesday attacked the Assembly, saying it wanted to go on a $4 billion "spending spree."

The Republican governor, who earlier this week blamed the need for a contingency budget on the Assembly, provided more detailed criticism of its proposed budget, though he told reporters in Albany he accepted its stand that apartment rent control rules would have to be dealt with in the new budget.

The June 15 expiry of rent control rules, which mainly affect New York City residents, were expected to be used to pressure Assembly Speaker Sheldon Silver, D-Manhattan. Pataki last year set a national record for late budgets by failing to get a pact for fiscal 1997 until 104 days after it was due.

The legislature by Wednesday was expected to approve the governor's $9.9 billion contingency budget that will provide enough money to keep New York State's government running from April 1 through May 9.

The governor, who has trumpeted his economic policies for creating new jobs, said the Democrat-led Assembly's proposed budget would derail the state's recovery by raising expenditures $4 billion above the amount he recommended.

"The Assembly Democrats will put a silver bullet through the heart of New York's recovery by returning to the blank-check, out-of-control budgets of the past. I will not allow them to recklessly spend, tax and borrow, placing our children's future in jeopardy," he said, in prepared remarks.
New York State's unemployment rate in February remained at 6.9 percent, though it gained more jobs than usual from the previous month, the state Department of Labor said on Tuesday.
A spokeswoman for the Assembly was not immediately available to respond to Pataki's blast.

Saying his priorities focused on welfare changes, school property tax relief, improving the state's economy and changing the criminal justice system, Pataki vowed not to let the Assembly forget big spending policies it and the former Cuomo Administration agreed in the late 1980s and early 1990s.

The legislature and the Pataki Administration failed to produce a consensus revenue estimate by a March 10 deadline, and as of late last week, stood about $1.3 billion apart, according to the state comptroller, H. Carl McCall.

The governor's specific criticisms of the Assembly's proposed budget included the lack of a plan to "break the cycle of welfare dependency," a failure to give all New York homeowners "double-digit" reductions in school property taxes and restrain their growth.

Pataki added the Assembly's proposed budget would not offer estate tax relief, a key part of his budget, create more prison beds needed due to stiffer sentencing rules or reform the juvenile justice system.
Whether residents of Staten Island, who would benefit from a proposal pushed by some lawmakers to cut express bus fares to Manhattan to $2 from $4, would get the lower fares, was not clear.

"I'm not sure, that's what we have to look at--everything from bond convenants to state subsidies to the impact on the overall plan," Pataki told reporters, when asked if cutting these fares would require Albany to help make up for the lost revenue.

A spokesman for the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, which is planning to help residents of New York City's outer bouroughs by ending two-zone fares, said "It's something that we continue to look at."
